chapter: String bands, serenading and violin players
title: Bowing versus picking the bass; the great bass player Pickaninny
summary: Dawson says he started the four-four rhythm on bass, used a bow for sentimental pieces and plucked for Dixieland, and praises Pickaninny who did both.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: He was good with a bow.
Well, who did? In fact, I, I'm the one who started that four-four rhythm with one thing. Uh-huh. You used to play with a bow too? Yeah. I was my main out with a bow. Yeah.
I, I still got my bow, yeah, too. Yeah.

Yeah. When did you, when did you change from playing bow to picking? Well, uh, you see, we, uh, the, we used to play a variety of music. We had class, we, we used to play class music, then we played Dixieland, you see. And there's certain pieces we played, it called for a bow, you see. Like, there was some, uh, sentimental pieces like that to me. And, uh, we used to have to use the bow. But, uh, all this Dixieland and jazz stuff, you play that good with a, with a bow. Uh, we had one fellow who was the bass, greatest bass player we ever had. I don't know, he died, a fella called Pickaninny.
Oh, you talk about a bass player, whoo!
Man, he, no, he played, he played with a bow, and he could pick too.
Yeah, but man, he couldn't, he couldn't master that bow too. Uh-huh. He could make all them double wraps and everything on the, on the bass.
